lines.note: Tirſe completes Par- on the preceding page, describing departure early or in haste. Tôcara deta supplies a past-tense example of having set out promptly.

runs.text: Ià hà pedaço que ſahio com preßa.

lines.note: The Portuguese explains that he left hurriedly some time ago. Initial Ià means already; the following verb is the historical ſahio, not the OCR’s ſabio.

runs.text: Particula, que ſe ajunta no cabo de outras

lines.note: Tô is the suffix meaning and so forth or the like, appended to other expressions. Its worn initial is T, matching the local alphabetical sequence, rather than F.

runs.text: palauras, como quẽ diz, &c. Eo de mais, ou

lines.note: The definition equates the suffix with et cetera and the rest. The printed Eo is retained without silently regularizing its spacing.
Goyôtô vôxe tçuqe- begins a deferential request to be assigned any business or other matters. The Japanese imperative is completed by rarei on the following row.

runs.text: Mandaime, que farei tudo o que vos

lines.note: Rarei completes the request to give an order; the Portuguese says to command the speaker, who will do whatever is needed.
Completes the promised service: whatever is required, and the rest. Comprir preserves the historical vowel of the Portuguese verb.
This separate Tô denotes rattan or Bengal cane. The example repeats Tô at the physical line end; it is unrelated to the preceding suffix.
Tô no tçuye is a cane staff or walking stick. The gloss explicitly specifies Bengal cane.

runs.text: Cabeça. mas não ſe vſa ſẽ al-

lines.note: Tô is explained by atama, head, and is said to occur in compounds. The faint initial T and the headword’s flush-left position are restored from the scan.
Gitô illustrates the compound use of the word for head; the next paragraph marker introduces an additional sense, continued below.
The additional meaning is the crust of a scab or skin lesion. Buſtella is retained as the printed historical form.

runs.text: Hũa piramide alta, ou torre de madeira.

lines.note: Tǒ denotes a tall wooden tower or pagoda, described as a high pyramid. The caron is distinct from the circumflex in the preceding Tô entries.

runs.text: Aue aßi chamada de cor vermelha.

lines.note: This homograph is described simply as a red bird of that name; the wording does not justify imposing a modern species identification.
Tǒ denotes the flower stalk or shoot of lettuce, mustard, and similar plants. The damaged middle of moſtarda contains the long s missing from OCR.

runs.text: Crecer o grelo, ou gomo das eruas.

lines.note: Tǒ ga tatçu means the stalk or shoot rising; the Portuguese describes the growth of the plant’s shoot or bud.
Qiri no tǒ illustrates the bud or flower of the kiri tree. The headword’s repeated r in Qiri below confirms the r-shaped letter misread as t in Qitino.
Re completes aruore; italic Qiri is the tree name embedded in the Portuguese explanation, not a fresh headword.
To is the connective translated as and or with. The Portuguese grammatical label is conjunction; the scan prints a colon after copulatiua.
The entry next gives the quotative use of to, classified here as Adu. Maittato mǒſu means reporting that someone has come.
Dizem que veo translates the preceding quotation: they say that he came. Veo is retained as the historical form.

runs.text: O aualiarſe, ou venderſe o arroz, &c.

lines.note: Toate denotes valuation or sale of rice at ten measures for a stated price. The gloss begins the explanation continued through the next rows.

runs.text: a dez medidas por algum certo preço. Vt,

lines.note: Specifies ten measures for some fixed price and introduces the example with italic Vt.
Comega toate ſuru states that the rice is valued at the rate described. The Portuguese phrase ends at dez and continues with medidas below.

runs.text: medidas por hũ maz, ou por algũ certo preço.

lines.note: Completes the price example as ten measures for one maz or another fixed price. The historical currency name and abbreviation tildes are preserved.
Tǒba is equated with Tǒ and defined as a tall wooden tower, continuing the pagoda sense encountered earlier.

Tǒbachi is referred to the preferred form Tǒbat and paraphrased by ataru bachi: punishment that befalls someone. The first caron is worn, but its surviving branch and the clear Tǒbachi cross-reference below favour this reading; the subsequently consulted NINJAL headword index (202510) agrees. Meliùs is the printed preference label.

runs.text: tigo, ou juſtiça que vem ſobre alguem.

lines.note: Completes caſtigo and adds justice coming upon a person, clarifying the punitive sense of bachi.
Tobai, with principal form bǒ, concerns a falcon launching itself or trying to break free. The following row completes the action.
Porſe ſoltar and voar describe freeing itself and flying; the phrase remains attached to the falcon entry.
Tobai cacari is given the same sense as the preceding falcon expression. The abbreviated principal form u is retained as printed.
Tǒban is a turn of guard duty, paraphrased by ataru ban, the watch that falls to someone. The gloss continues with pertence below.

Completes the sense of a watch belonging to a person; Tǒbande gozaru means that it is one’s turn on duty. The small mark above o is faint but has a downward-pointing shape, supporting the chosen caron; it is less clear than the headword’s mark above.
Tǒbari is defined as a Chinese needle. The downward mark over o is a caron, unlike the OCR circumflex.

runs.text: O porſe atraueſado na porta pera não

lines.note: Tobari here means standing across a doorway so as to prevent passage. It is distinct from the preceding long-vowel needle entry.
Completes the obstruction of someone’s passage and gives Tobariuo ſuru as the expression for doing so.
Tǒbat refers back to Tǒbachi, the punishment entry. The downward marks, particularly the clear one in the cross-reference, support carons rather than the OCR’s first circumflex.
Tobatçuqi and the alternative Tofatçuqu concern restless or bustling activity. The Japanese f in the alternative is not the long s of a Portuguese word.

runs.text: ou andarinquieto, ou com eſtrondo, & traqui-

lines.note: The gloss describes being restless, noisy, and engaged in commotion. Traqui- continues as traquinada on the next physical row.
Completes traquinada and begins adjectival examples with Tobatçuqu or Tobatçuita modifying mono across the line break.
No completes mono: a restless or flustered person. The Portuguese qualification continues below.
Em fazer as couſas limits the preceding description to the way the person performs tasks, completing the entry.
Tobera is identified simply as a tree of that name. The brief gloss does not itself provide a botanical classification.

runs.text: Quantidade, ou porção que ſe toma por

lines.note: Tobet denotes a quantity or portion taken for each ten measures, with the measure context supplied in the following row.

runs.text: cada dez medidas que ſe medẽ, ou dão darroz.

lines.note: Completes the assessment on each ten measures of rice measured or distributed. The damaged d of medidas corrects the OCR’s spurious internal space.
Tobi is the bird glossed as minhoto, a kite. This noun is separate from the verb beginning on the next line.
Tobi, bu, ôda gives the principal forms of the verb for flying, with a second sense of jumping. The scan supplies the missing i and the accented ôda; the historical principal part is not modernized.

zones.label: Column 2 running header
zones.note: The right running header prints ATES without N; this source anomaly is retained.

lines.note: Tobiagari denotes flying high or upward. The row closes with a period after cima, not the OCR’s line-end hyphen.
Tobiariqi describes going about by flying or hopping. The printed principal part uita is retained as historical morphology.

runs.text: ſaltando como coruos. ¶ Item, per met.

lines.note: The comparison is to crows hopping or flying about; the next clause explicitly begins a figurative application.

runs.text: O andar como ſaltando, ou inquieto como mi-

lines.note: The figurative sense is restless or hopping movement, with the comparison to children completed below.
Ninos completes mininos, mischievous children, illustrating the restless behaviour described in the preceding rows.
Tobicacari means flying or leaping at something. The Portuguese begins an explanation of striking down upon an object.

runs.text: gũa couſa como minhoto, &c. mas mais

lines.note: A kite is the initial comparison; mais begins the qualification that this expression is used more properly in another context.

runs.text: propriamente ſe diz de homem, ou animal q̃

lines.note: The preferred context is a person or animal attacking another. The final q̃ is a printed abbreviation and is not expanded.

runs.text: dà ſobre outro, ou arremete com furia.

lines.note: Completes the description as falling upon another or charging furiously, explaining the forceful sense of tobicacari.
Tobicaqeri means flying through the air; Sorauo begins an example with the sky or air as its object. The abbreviated principal form ta is preserved as printed.
Tobicaqeru tori completes the phrase for birds flying through the sky; the Portuguese translates it directly as birds flying through the air.
Tobicayeri first means returning in flight. A further sense of rebounding or springing back follows.

runs.text: Tornar, & ſaltar pera tras como ſeta que dà

lines.note: Explains returning or jumping backward like an arrow that strikes something. The object of dà continues below.
Nalgũa pedra completes the arrow example: striking a stone and rebounding. It is a separate physical continuation row.
Tobichiri means scattering in flight. The Portuguese word diuerſas is physically divided after di-.

runs.text: uerſas partes. ¶ Item, Saltar, ou bulir

lines.note: Completes the scattering into various directions, then adds the sense of jumping or moving about a great deal.
Completes the restless-motion sense as moving a great deal from here to there. The grave accents in cà and là are retained.
Tobicoye is passing over something in flight, with the obstacle examples supplied on the next row.
Mountains and trees illustrate what is crossed or flown over. The abbreviated plural dalgũs remains unexpanded.
Tobicudari denotes descending by flying or, as completed below, jumping down. Decer preserves the historical Portuguese spelling.
Saltando supplies the alternative manner of descent, jumping, and completes the preceding definition.
Tobifaxiri is running at full speed. The gloss continues with the combination of jumping and running below.
Saltar and correr complete the vigorous-motion sense of the preceding verb; the short continuation is not a new entry.
Tobifi is a flying spark of fire. Here fi means fire, and the Portuguese describes a spark that jumps.
Tobiiuo and tobivuo are alternative names for the flying fish. The printed internal i/u/v spellings are retained independently.
Tobimeguri describes moving in circles, specifically in flight as completed by the following word.
Voando completes the circling-flight definition, remaining a separate physical row.

runs.text: Hum bichinho aßi chamado que ſal-

lines.note: Tobimuxi is a small insect described through its jumping movement. The definition does not require identification beyond the named insect.
Ta completes ſalta, and the comparison is to a flea. This is a description of motion, not an assertion that the insect is itself a flea.

runs.text: Hũs bules, ou fraſcos de metal que ſer-

lines.note: Tǒbin names metal pots or flasks; their purpose is specified on the next line. The marked o is preserved as a caron.
Completes the use of the vessels for holding hot water. Agoa, visible in the crop, corrects OCR agon without modernizing to agua.
Tobinoqi describes moving away by flying or jumping. The principal part oita supports the -noqi stem; the abraded round vowel is o, not OCR e.
Fastarſe completes afastarſe across the line boundary, explaining movement away from a place or object.
Tǒbiǒ is paraphrased as saxiataru yamai, the illness currently affecting someone. Both marked o vowels retain their printed carons.
Ou dagora restates the sense as the present or current illness. It is the completion of the preceding gloss.
Tobiǒxi denotes rattling ritual instruments, glossed as sestros, which certain women play. The description of these performers follows.
The women are called Mico and play before the Cami. Both Japanese terms occur inside the Portuguese explanation; To- begins the separate example at the right edge.
Biǒxiuo auaſuru completes the example for playing these instruments; the Portuguese begins its equivalent with tanger and tocar.
Sestros names the instruments again and completes the translation. Its visible indentation is restored; it is a short continuation, not a new headword.
Tobira is a hinged or pivoted door, described by Portuguese porta de couceira.
Tobiſagari means descending in flight, parallel to the earlier tobicudari entry.
Tobiſari describes a bird rising or taking flight. The Portuguese explanation continues on the next line.
Ou acolherſe voando adds the sense of retreating or making away in flight.
Tobitachi is rising into flight. The entry then develops a figurative use referring to the heart.
Cocoro tobitatçu describes the heart leaping with joy; the Portuguese begins alegrar-se, rejoicing. The damaged r in Alegrar- corrects OCR Alegiar-.

runs.text: ſe muito, ou ſaltar de prazer.

lines.note: Completes alegrar-se as being very joyful or jumping for pleasure. The second expression makes the figurative connection to flight and jumping explicit.
Tobivatari means passing to another place in flight. The printed v in vatari represents wa; OCR y would obscure the verb wataru.
